A fine movie, but I believe that it certainly could've been better than it was, had it more true to Alexandra Rippley's book.

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a drunken Swedish book editor who's stuck on a train from Stockholm to Berlin. According to everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. There's also a wealthy man and his mistress, a woman trying to find her husband (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, a couple of gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two gangsters, a group of refugees, and even a nun. Meant as a mix of noir and thriller (which it does quite well), it tries to experiment with comedy and drama, and it fails with both. It doesn't sit well with the change in tone with every new scene, and as the train gets closer to its destination, the film gets more and more absurd, ending on a very surreal note. A good cast is wasted on a myriad of weak plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the director called everyone he's ever worked with and gave them a part in the film. Of course, the actors are only as good as the script they're given them - don't blame them. The comedy is too forced and unfunny, and the drama is too over the top. The pacing is painfully slow at times (quite a few times), with one scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to rely on swearing and crude profendo to avoid decent dialogue. The film looks good though, in spite of cinematography and cinematography. Overall, this film fails in almost every department. 3/10

I think he would be well served by a film about his life.

Trite and uninspired. It's like someone took Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them all together, with the added bonus of stealing just enough plot points from two movies to make another one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some historical facts that are manipulated to better fit the story. This is understandable for the most part. For example, during the early part of Beethoven's life, it was common for deaf people to write down what they needed to say in order for others to understand them. This, of course, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, while filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the spirit of that time. This, coupled with the bad acting, seems rather glaring. The lead actor is talented enough, but I hope he still has time to work on his craft. If you're really looking for something about Beethoven, don't blame Gary Ross for this film. Instead, read a biography or one of the many other films about Beethoven. Or just immerse yourself in the music of the great composer. http://iwascalledclementine.blogspot.com/

This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-September attachments, doubtless what is on the mind of the elder party is either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind parent that she (or he) lacked as a child. These underlying agendas seem more pathetic than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well he should--at playing the elder lover in this silly story. He was, at fifty, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. This bit of romantic comedy is typical of the kind of story I enjoyed as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of younger-older relationships, the motivation is on the part of the elder is usually either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both, while the younger is most likely looking for the kind of energy and vigor that they lacked as a child. Such hidden agendas seem more sinister than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit tired--as well he could be--as the hero of this rather silly story. He was, at least, attempting the role of a thirty-five-year-old man romancing a seventeen-year-old. But Vivgrid Chapman was a revelation--pretty, intelligent, and full of charm--as the heroine, the seventeen-year-old presented as a gift to "The Man," the morally upright and honest screenwriter, as a subject for him to film. Her strong performance wrung from Powell a bit more than the film would otherwise deserve. Anna Lee was excellent as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and handled her small part deftly. There is some rather funny dialogue in the film, too, so it's not a complete washout. 5/10

Who the hell is responsible for this terrible mangling of one of my favorite books? This is just terrible. The mean, the editing. The book isn't even close to its old self. And what were they thinking? Robin Williams, for Gosh's sake! This movie defies logic. If you see it, please, don't. Not even the laughs are worth it if you're a fan of the book. This might just be the worst movie adaptation ever - everything is disjointed, all of the details that are necessary in order to understand the book's themes are completely ignored, and every potentially interesting moment in the book has been changed (example: moving to New York) into something absurd and pointless. For those who haven't read the book, it's basically a simple story about a boy growing up and watching his mother struggle in life. His mother writes an autobiography, which eventually (despite her efforts) becomes a sort of feminist manifesto. The book is well-written, poignant, and tells a story that's both beautiful and sad. The movie, on the other hand, is about Robin Williams once again telling jokes to save the day.

Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are unnecessary shots to an audience watching the clips and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are among audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we love horror films. Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of ten classic horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are occasional shots to an audience watching these films. Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are the audience members who talk to the camera and explain why they love these films. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("film horror makes us afraid of real horror", "we're at the mercy of the filmmaker in the theatre") and pretty trite. All the films are shown very quickly and the transitions are kind of jarring. Also, seven out of the ten films shown aren't very scary at all and the film is very short. I saw this in the theater back in 1984 and was annoyed that I paid $7.50 for an hour of mostly boring films. Still, it's a well-produced film and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. So if you have an interest in the history of terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored and think it's a bad scare (no pun intended). I give it a C.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but it unfortunately does not deliver on just that. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically relaxed in his scenes in his usual attire, which he trades in for a sort of Indian garb to meet the daughter of the mysterious Lord Rylott (Lyn Harding). It's not clear in the picture why Rylott would have wanted his daughter to meet Holmes. If as was the case with Helen (played by Joaninemore), he didn't want her to run off to marry Holmes, he would have accomplished the same thing by having Holmes leave. The cabinet of curiosities may to have way of setting an example for Holmes with Helen, but Rylott is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The inclusion of a cabinet of curiosities as the cause of Rylott's death is merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting plot tool, a deadly snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not shown at point in the picture. However, the Indian garb notwithstanding, Raymond Massey's performance is a good representation of Holmes' laid-back and confident demeanor, and has some of the charm of Nigel Bruce's performance in the original film. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is surprisingly menacing, a trait that would be used in his portrayal of Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two other films, 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Hound at the Baskervilles." With a lack of budget and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is still maintained, even if it stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I suppose that would be the case even with the snake, though, as one of the first cuts in the picture proved to be the one bringing in the asp.

Put simply, this mini-series was terrible. Let me count the ways: 1. Over-acting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Overly-top approach to storytelling. 4. Over-the-top narration. 5. Very little to nothing of interest. This film can't even be called "Soap Opera" because it's that bad. Now, it's not a Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, so I'm judging it only as a film, and it really stinks. Imagine going to a party and they give you dozens of candies. You marvel at the wide variety and start to taste them, but suddenly they're all gone and you wonder where they went. It's like this film, with far too many characters who are not drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a full-length film or two, yet we are given less than two hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions and reaction shots of the characters than you'll find in 10,000 monkeys jumping at a wall in slow motion. David Hurt and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent train metaphor is trite. And, perhaps the most ridiculous character in the film---the cat. This angry, vengeful cat who follows the hero around to scratch him and his seat covers. Oh, come on now---this isn't even the Lion King! Perhaps the most interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn out, is John Voss, the disturbed boy whose final act of desperation accounts for the majority of the real drama in this film. Otherwise, just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there is little here to inspire. The drama is mostly melodrama, and the acting is terrible.

Though a fan of horror and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The makeup and puppet effects were good, yes, and the scares was well-timed, but the pacing was terrible. Firstly, the first act of the movie is spent learning all of Jack Brooks' backstory, despite the fact that everything we needed to know was revealed in the first few minutes of the opening title sequence. Thus, the narration and most of the flashbacks were needless. The majority of the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then sleeping, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the only action is a few-minute montage of Jack trying to hit Freddy with his chair. (Definitely an entertaining moment in the film, excellent for getting a few laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack manages to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: The New Nightmare had loads of potential but its poor pacing and unnecessary exposition kept it from an adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell and Jack vs. Ash go into production.

Although I knew from the trailer that the film was bad (BAD IDEA!), I went ahead and watched it anyway. *What the heck.* This movie is a joke. First off, the acting of the "parents" sucks, and the scene where "Jake" (main character) is in the farm looks fake, and the buildings even look fake. Now we get to the house, where the "man" (I think he's the father, but I don't know) is in there. And then, all of a sudden, they start to get attacked by (gasp) A FREAKIN SCARECROW! AHHH! This movie is the definition of low budget, and the scenes where the scarecrow is attacking looks so fake it's ridiculous. It has fake eyes and everything! And then at the end...they shoot the scarecrow with a gun (that, for f***'s sake, looks like it was bought at a local family dollar store), it pauses for a while and then.....(gasp) dies. This movie will waste some time, I'm telling you this. So, if you want to waste an hour and a half, look at the trailer, and know that the it is a far lie compared to the movie. It is quite funny, though. Grade: *If there was anything lower (F-), Dark Harvest would get it.*
